opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few ways to look at it.

The simplest is leverage. If you're a company spending billions of dollars a year on compute, the question is whether that compute is used well. One researcher with good judgment, who knows which experiment to run, which direction is a dead end, or how to make training stable at scale, can change the efficiency of that whole investment by a meaningful percentage. Next to the compute bill, even a very large salary is small. From the company's side it's a rational calculation, not a bubble in people.

The second reason is scarcity of a particular kind of experience. Frontier model training is a skill you mostly learn by doing it, at scale, inside one of a handful of labs. It's not in papers. A lot of it is tacit knowledge: intuition about data, about scaling behavior, about what breaks when you go from one size to the next. Only a small number of people have touched those systems end to end, so the supply is very thin while demand jumped almost overnight.

Third, there's a strategic and somewhat defensive element. When the race is perceived as winner-take-most, hiring someone is also about making sure your competitor doesn't have them. That pushes prices beyond pure productivity value. It's a bit like a transfer market in sports.

That said, I'd be careful about over-reading it. Valuation of individuals reflects how uncertain the field is. Nobody fully knows which ideas will matter next, so companies pay a premium for people who've been right before. But research is still very much a team activity, and the infrastructure, the data, and the culture around a person matter a lot. Someone who's very productive in one environment won't automatically be equally productive in another.

So my honest view: the prices are mostly explainable by compute leverage and scarcity, with some extra from competitive dynamics. Whether they stay this high depends on whether the knowledge stays this concentrated. As it diffuses, which it always does eventually, I'd expect things to normalize somewhat.

r001.rationale: The response says frontier training is learned by doing it at scale in a handful of labs, and only a small number of people have that experience.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes research as a team activity and says productivity depends on the surrounding infrastructure, data, and culture.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest answer is that it's a supply-and-demand mismatch, but the more interesting answer is about what kind of scarcity it is.

If you look at the whole field, there are actually a lot of people who can do AI research. Every year thousands of PhDs graduate, NeurIPS has tens of thousands of attendees. So it's not that researchers in general are scarce. What's scarce is a very specific thing: people who have actually been in the loop of training frontier models and have intuition about what works at scale. That knowledge is almost entirely tacit. It doesn't live in papers, because the labs stopped publishing the important details. It lives in a few hundred people who have watched a lot of runs fail and developed a sense for why. You can't learn that from the outside, and you can't speed it up by reading more. So the pool is small and it regenerates slowly.

Then on the demand side, the stakes became enormous. When I was doing my PhD, if a research direction turned out to be wrong, you lost a paper. Now if a lab makes a wrong bet on data mixture or RL setup, you can burn hundreds of millions of dollars of compute and fall half a year behind. In that situation, paying someone tens of millions is cheap if they shift your probability of making the right call by even a few percent. The salary is a rounding error relative to the compute budget it's protecting. So the valuation isn't really about the person's output in the traditional sense. It's an insurance premium on very expensive decisions.

There's also a feedback effect that I think people underestimate. Because the top labs are so concentrated, a researcher moving from one to another is not just adding talent to the destination, they're removing it from the competitor and carrying information with them. So you're paying for a two-sided effect. That's unusual in most industries.

That said, I'd be a bit careful about reading the numbers as a measure of individual genius. A lot of it is being in the right place at the right time, with access to compute and to colleagues who were also learning fast. I happened to work on agents and reasoning when those became central, and I'm very aware that if I'd picked a different topic in 2020, nobody would be asking me this question. So I think the honest framing is: the market is rationally pricing a scarce, hard-to-transfer resource during a window where mistakes are extremely costly. Whether that window stays open for a long time, I'm genuinely not sure. As tools and infrastructure mature, a lot of today's tacit knowledge gets codified, and then the premium should come down. It's happened in every previous technology wave.

r001.rationale: It says the scarce group is people who have trained frontier models and gained tacit, hands-on experience, and that this pool is small and regenerates slowly.

r002.rationale: It describes researchers learning alongside colleagues and explains that moving between concentrated labs transfers information while affecting both teams, presenting research as a collective endeavor.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two forces at work. One is the expectation that AI will create enormous economic value. The other is that the people who can meaningfully improve the best models are still relatively scarce. If a company believes a better model could be worth billions of dollars, paying a lot for someone who might help produce that improvement can seem rational.

But research is hard to evaluate. Results depend on a team, compute, data, infrastructure, and sometimes luck. It’s difficult to isolate one person’s contribution, so companies also compete on signals like reputation and previous affiliations. That can push compensation beyond what anyone can confidently justify.

So I’d distinguish the value of AI from the value attributed to an individual researcher. The first can be very large while the second is still uncertain. Over time, I’d expect the market to get better at identifying who can consistently turn research ideas into actual progress.

r001.rationale: The response says people able to improve the best models are scarce, but does not attribute that scarcity to few opportunities to gain AI research experience.

r002.rationale: The response describes results as depending on a team alongside compute, data, infrastructure, and luck, characterizing research as collective.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the market is pricing in two things: the potential impact of AI, and the scarcity of people who can reliably push it forward. If a researcher can meaningfully improve a model that serves millions of users, even a small improvement can have enormous economic value. And research isn’t something where you can simply hire ten times as many people and get ten times the progress. Judgment matters a lot—choosing the right problem, knowing which experiments to run, and recognizing when a result is important.

But compensation is also a bet on the future. It reflects what companies think AI could become, not just the value researchers are producing today. So I wouldn’t interpret a high salary as an objective ranking of someone’s intelligence or scientific contribution. It’s a market price shaped by scarcity, competition, and expectations—and those expectations can be wrong.

r001.rationale: The response mentions a scarcity of people who can advance AI, but does not attribute that scarcity to relatively few people having had opportunities to gain AI research experience.

r002.rationale: The response discusses individual researchers’ judgment and impact, but does not characterize AI research as a collective endeavor.
